source: Brown, Imai, Vieider, Camerer (2022 version) Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion
finding: Loss aversion is real on average but smaller than the classic 2.25. Best pooled estimate is about 1.95.
numbers: 607 estimates from 150 articles (1992-2017). Bayesian random-effects mean lambda 1.955, 95% CrI [1.820, 2.105]. Raw data: mean 1.97, median 1.69 (522 usable estimates). A simple normal model gives 1.809 [1.740, 1.878].
limits: Dominated by published studies. Many lab tasks are unincentivized or hypothetical. Estimates depend on how lambda is defined.
agent_relevance: If we ever give the agent a loss weight, about 1.7-2.0 is the empirical anchor, not 2.25.

source: Brown et al. meta-analysis, heterogeneity section
finding: Study design explains little of the variation in loss aversion estimates.
numbers: Covariates explain only 15.5% of between-observation variance. Benchmark study lambda 1.984 [1.593, 2.385]. Field experiments and general-population samples give higher lambda than student lab samples. Money vs non-money rewards: no difference. Functional form and reference point (zero, status quo, expectations): little difference. Survey studies lower than binary-lottery tasks. Individual-level means (mean 2.94, SD 2.61) run higher than individual-level medians (mean 1.84, SD 0.76).
limits: Coded features are crude. Only one study (Chapman et al. 2018) reports IQ links: median lambda 0.99 in a US representative survey vs 1.84 in a college sample with a similar protocol.
agent_relevance: Loss weight is not a fixed trait. Treat any single value as context bound.

source: Brown et al. meta-analysis, publication bias section
finding: There is modest evidence that high lambda values are more likely to be published.
numbers: Bias-corrected mean lambda 1.742 [1.674, 1.811] vs 1.955 uncorrected. Unpublished working papers about 0.25 lower (about 1.73). Authors suggest 1.73-1.74 for bias-wary users. Original Tversky and Kahneman 1992 median 2.25 came from 25 graduate students, unincentivized. Conference audience guesses for the mean averaged 1.639 (SD 0.599, 34 answers).
limits: No single test for publication bias fits a bounded, skewed parameter.
agent_relevance: Even the headline effect shrinks about 11% after bias correction. Single-study numbers should not be trusted.

source: Ruggeri et al. (2020) Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk, Nature Human Behaviour 4:622-633
finding: Large preregistered multinational replication of the 1979 paper. Core patterns hold up, with attenuation.
numbers: N = 4,098 (abstract), 19 countries, 13 languages. Results replicated for 94% of items. 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated. Some countries showed 100% replication. Heterogeneity between countries and within individuals.
quote: We conclude that the empirical foundations for prospect theory replicate beyond any reasonable thresholds.
limits: Only the abstract and reference list were readable (paywalled). Item-level effect sizes and the one failed contrast were not read. Hypothetical choices with local-currency conversion.
agent_relevance: Qualitative PT anomalies (certainty effect, reflection, framing) are among the sturdiest in behavioural science, so an LLM copying them is not surprising.

source: Walasek and Stewart (2015) How to make loss aversion disappear and reverse: decision by sampling origin of loss aversion, JEP:General 144:7-11
finding: Loss aversion depends on the range of gains and losses offered in the task. It can vanish or reverse.
numbers: Exp 1a N=358 (MTurk, 323 kept); Exp 1b N=423 (382 kept); Exp 2 N=429 (401 kept); Exp 3 N=88 lab with real money. 50-50 mixed gambles, accept or reject. Median lambda with gains up to 40 and losses up to 20: 1.79 [1.55, 2.00] (Exp 1a), 1.59 (1b), 2.28 (Exp 2, gains 3x loss range), 1.81 (Exp 3). Symmetric ranges: about 1.00-1.02. Losses range wider than gains: 0.88, 0.81, 0.93 (reversal). In Exp 2 the reverse condition was about 1.01, not below 1 as predicted.
quote: We were able to find loss aversion, loss neutrality, and even the reverse of loss aversion.
limits: Mostly hypothetical MTurk lotteries. Reversal was weaker in Exp 2. Linear value function assumed. The 40-20 condition replicates the Tom et al. task (median 1.93).
agent_relevance: Loss aversion in a stimulus set may reflect the distribution of numbers shown. When we test an LLM, match gain and loss ranges.

source: Rakow, Cheung, Restelli (2020) Losing my loss aversion: effects of current and past environment on relative sensitivity to losses, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review
finding: Replicates the range effect in two sessions. Shows modest within-person stability and carry-over from earlier stakes.
numbers: 64 mixed gambles per session, two sessions. About three-quarters of participants were loss averse when gains had the wider range (every 95% CI for the median lambda excluded values below 1). Most showed reverse loss aversion when losses had the wider range. Loss aversion fell in session 2 after higher stakes in session 1.
limits: Explanations also include expected-value rank within the choice set and adaptive aspirations, not only decision by sampling. Sample size not extracted.
agent_relevance: Past context shifts later loss weighting, an echo of in-context effects in LLMs.

source: Mukherjee (2019) Revise the belief in loss aversion, Frontiers in Psychology 10:2723
finding: Critical review. Loss aversion is used both as a principle and as evidence for itself, and several phenomena once credited to it have rival explanations.
numbers: Lists challenges: status quo bias (Gal), endowment effect (Morewedge and Giblin; Yechiam), risky-bet premium (Ert and Erev; Yechiam and Hochman), hedonic impact (Harinck; Mukherjee). Affect studies: losses did not hurt as predicted when experienced (Kermer et al.); gains loomed equal or larger for small amounts and losses larger for large amounts.
limits: Short opinion piece. Cites others for numbers. No pooled effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Circular use of loss aversion warns us not to read LLM loss-averse answers as evidence of an internal loss weight.

source: Litovsky, Loewenstein, Horn, Olivola (2022) Loss aversion, the endowment effect, and gain-loss framing shape preferences for noninstrumental information, PNAS
finding: Prospect-theory patterns extend to information that has no money value.
numbers: Study 1: gamble less likely when the same outcome is framed as a loss of information. Study 2: endowment effect for information. Study 3: Asian-disease style pattern with facts instead of lives. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. Effects were for noninstrumental trivia, not real decisions.
agent_relevance: Shows reference dependence is general across goods, so it is plausible as a strong prior in training text.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory (COLM)
finding: Prospect-theory fits for 9 LLMs. Only GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo passed a basic consistency test on the gambling game.
numbers: Models: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-2 7B/13B/70B, Mistral 7B, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 2.1. 56 game settings, 100 samples per setting at temperature 1. GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo: no probability distortion for gains. GPT-4 Turbo: stronger distortion than humans for losses, overweights small probabilities. Overall: weaker loss aversion and similar risk aversion vs humans.
limits: Competence test is a monotone switching point. Claude 2.1 and the others failed it, so they were not fitted. Old model versions.
agent_relevance: Most LLMs are not coherent enough in gamble choice to fit PT at all. Consistency enforcement in the scaffold matters more than any PT bias.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024), prompting interventions on GPT-4 risk and loss aversion
finding: Telling GPT-4 to be risk or loss averse did not move behaviour reliably. One example helped. Two examples got confounded.
numbers: 56 settings, N=10 samples. Direct instruction: no reliable change; for losses the value function became unexpectedly non-convex. One-shot example worked for risk-averse and loss-averse targets. Two-shot gave mixed results. Role-play as teenager or senior: less loss averse, no change in risk aversion; advice-giving mode gave different shifts than role-play.
limits: One model (GPT-4), one task family.
agent_relevance: Risk attitude is poorly steerable by instruction alone. Worked examples work better than rules.

source: Wang, Lin, Liu et al. (2025/2026) Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs: instability of decision-making under epistemic uncertainty
finding: Prospect theory does not fit every LLM. Larger models fit better but loss aversion stays unstable.
numbers: Human benchmark (Tanaka et al. 2010): alpha 0.670, lambda 2.630, gamma 0.685. Baseline LLM fits (alpha, lambda, gamma, MAE, McFadden R2): Llama-3.1-8B 0.585, 0.010, 0.753, 0.332, 0.092; Qwen2.5-7B 0.429, 0.010, 3.645, 0.047, 0.116; Qwen2.5-14B 0.503, 1.909, 0.896, 0.257, 0.067; Qwen2.5-32B 0.598, 1.213, 0.867, 0.161, 0.225; GPT-5-Mini 0.447, 4.000, 2.888, 0.115, 0.206. Reliable fit means MAE <= 0.20 and R2 >= 0.10. Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B failed both.
limits: Columns read from a two-column PDF, so alignment is likely but not certain. Binary choices with exact probabilities. Lambda 0.010 and 4.000 are optimizer bounds.
agent_relevance: Do not report PT parameters for an LLM without a fit check. Boundary lambda values mean the model is not reference-dependent.

source: Wang et al. (2025/2026), epistemic markers experiment
finding: Replacing numeric probabilities with words such as 'likely' shifts PT parameters, especially loss aversion.
numbers: 14 epistemic markers mapped to implied probabilities by indifference point. Marker ordering (almost certain above highly likely above unlikely) is consistent across models. Four rounds placed markers on option K, on all series, on option U only, or on both. Risk curvature stays near 0.4-0.6 for larger models. Loss aversion shifts most across rounds. Larger models (Qwen2.5-32B) were more robust.
limits: Absolute marker probabilities differ across models. Per-round values not tabulated here.
agent_relevance: Verbal uncertainty in prompts changes risk behaviour. Links to the Verbal confidence subfield.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara, Chen (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs under uncertain context (NeurIPS)
finding: Estimated risk, probability weighting and loss aversion for three commercial LLMs, then added demographic personas.
numbers: ChatGPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.0-pro; 300 repeated runs per model; multiple-choice-list task. All three risk averse. ChatGPT: lowest loss aversion, probability weighting parameter above 1 (unlike humans). Claude: lower risk aversion, higher loss aversion, overweights small probabilities. Persona effects: Claude more conservative for sexual-minority or disabled personas; Gemini higher loss aversion for younger or rural personas.
limits: Table numbers were garbled by extraction, so exact lambdas are not recorded. Persona effects are differences across 10 groups, not compared to human data.
agent_relevance: Persona text moves risk preference. A schema should not let role text silently set risk attitude.

source: Corazzini, Deriu, Guerzoni (2025) Decision and gender biases in LLMs: a behavioral-economic perspective
finding: Gemma-7B and Qwen-2.5-32B show mild loss aversion in a gambling game. Gender labels change nothing in the gamble task.
numbers: Estimates for one model (gambling game): gain curvature 1.062 (near risk neutral), gain weighting 1.001, loss curvature 0.932, loss weighting 0.800, lambda 1.542. Human benchmarks cited: alpha about 0.88, lambda 2.25. Male and female prompts gave near-identical estimates.
limits: Two small open models. Which model the quoted table belongs to was not checked.
agent_relevance: Small open LLMs lean toward risk neutral gains and weaker loss aversion than the 2.25 benchmark.

source: Saeedi, Goodarzi, Canbaz (2025) Heuristics and biases in AI decision-making: implications for responsible AGI
finding: 1,500 experiments over nine biases in GPT-4o, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1. Answers contradict across gain and loss framings in most cases.
numbers: Contradictory answers to positive vs negative framing of identical scenarios in 57% (GPT-4o), 74% (Gemma 2), 85% (Llama 3.1). Llama 3.1 refused to support a scenario in positive framing in over 44% of cases. GPT-4o best overall; Gemma 2 strong on sunk cost and prospect theory; Llama 3.1 weakest.
limits: Author-defined scoring. Few prompts per bias. Preprint v3.
agent_relevance: Frames flip LLM answers. A check that states the problem both ways can catch it.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT shows a gain-loss framing effect, like people.
numbers: ChatGPT: 11 trials per frame; rated drug efficacy 5 in all 11 gain-frame trials and 4 in all 11 loss-frame trials (1-7 scale). Humans (82 MTurk master workers, 44 gain and 39 loss): 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37) vs 4.6 (4.35-4.85), t(80) = 3.86, p < 0.001.
limits: Rating task, not a risky choice. Zero variance across ChatGPT trials. Authors suggest language associations, not loss aversion, may drive it.
agent_relevance: An LLM framing effect can come from word patterns, so do not read it as value-function curvature.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3, PNAS
finding: GPT-3 reproduced three of six Kahneman and Tversky 1979 anomalies.
numbers: Replicated K&T problem pairs using choice probabilities. Found framing effect, certainty effect, and overweighting of small-probability differences (1% vs 2% counts more than 41% vs 42%). Did not show the other three of six.
limits: Which three were absent was not read. GPT-3 (2022). Hypothetical choices.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that PT anomalies appear in LLM text choices with no training aimed at them.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT, PNAS
finding: GPT's budget choices are more consistent than human choices, but consistency breaks under price re-framing.
numbers: 25 budget tasks per domain, 100 GPT observations. Zero GARP violations: 95 (risk), 89 (time), 81 (social), 92 (food). Mean CCEI 0.998, 0.997, 0.997, 0.999 vs humans 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. Literature mean CCEI 0.918 (range 0.81-0.99). Under price re-framing: risk CCEI 0.901 (34% below 0.9), time 0.884, social 0.698 (88% below 0.9), food 0.894.
limits: Continuous budget task, not PT-style binary gambles. Preference parameters are more homogeneous than humans'.
agent_relevance: LLMs can be rational in a clean format and incoherent after a surface change. Supports format-robustness checks.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias, TACL
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase the certainty effect and other biases.
numbers: Certainty-effect bias score (target choice rate in treatment minus control; higher is more bias): GPT-3 DaVinci-002 0.24, DaVinci-003 0.67; T5 0.09 vs Flan-T5 0.17. Abstract: stronger bias in instruction-tuned Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
limits: Table partly garbled in extraction. Certainty effect is one of three biases studied.
agent_relevance: Post-training pushes toward human-like certainty preference. Do not assume a risk-neutral base.

source: Ge, Zhang, Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the gap: a contrast in risky choices between reasoning and conversational language models (ACL 2026)
finding: Reasoning models act close to expected-payoff maximizers. Conversational models are less rational and sensitive to order, framing and explanations.
numbers: 20 frontier and open LLMs vs a rational agent and 360 US Prolific participants. 3 base prospect pairs shown as descriptions and as simulated histories of 20 and 100 samples. All models show a description-history gap, larger for conversational models. Maths-reasoning training is the likely cause (open-model comparison).
limits: Read only a mirror-site abstract page, not the paper. No numeric effects given. Verify against the ACL paper before citing.
agent_relevance: Supports our scaffold idea: explicit reasoning steps pull LLM risky choice toward expected value and away from framing.

source: Wulff, Mergenthaler-Canseco, Hertwig (2018) A meta-analytic review of two modes of learning and the description-experience gap, Psychological Bulletin 144:140-176
finding: Meta-analysis of the description-experience gap: rare events tend to be underweighted when learned by experience and overweighted when described.
numbers: Not read this session. Numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Title confirmed through Europe PMC listing only. Check effect sizes before use.
agent_relevance: Parallels the description vs history gap in Ge et al.

source: Gal and Rucker (2018) The loss of loss aversion: will it loom larger than its gain? Journal of Consumer Psychology
finding: Critique arguing the evidence for loss aversion is weaker than assumed, with other mechanisms such as inertia or attention behind many results.
numbers: Not read this session. Numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Mukherjee (2019) cites Gal and Rucker as the call for a critical look.
agent_relevance: Another reason to treat loss weight as context bound.

source: Yechiam (2019) Acceptable losses: the debatable origins of loss aversion, Psychological Research 83:1327-1339
finding: Argues loss aversion is not universal and is often absent for small stakes.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Not opened. Known from the citation in Mukherjee (2019) and a Europe PMC title match.
agent_relevance: Same as above.

source: Hertwig, Wulff, Mata (2019) Three gaps and what they may mean for risk preference, Phil Trans R Soc B
finding: Risk preference measured by description, experience and self-reported propensity correlates weakly across measures.
numbers: Not read this session. Full text in Europe PMC returned empty.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A single 'risk attitude' may not exist for a human or an agent. Keep it per task.

source: Brown et al. meta-analysis, distribution of raw estimates
finding: Reported loss aversion estimates are right skewed. Aggregate-level estimates sit lowest, individual-level means highest.
numbers: Aggregate-level n=281: mean 1.950, median 1.520. Individual-level means n=160: mean 2.935, median 1.800. Individual-level medians n=166: mean 1.844. All 522: mean 1.970, median 1.690, range 0.04 to 23.46. Among 85 studies with both: mean of means 3.47, mean of medians 1.71.
limits: Choice of mean vs median matters more than design details. Extreme values are a few outlying studies.
agent_relevance: Report medians and intervals for any LLM loss-aversion estimate, not single means.
